Seoul Street Food Guide 2026: What to Eat & Where to Find It

The complete guide to Seoul street food — tteokbokki, hotteok, tornado potatoes, and everything else you need to eat at least once in Seoul.

⏱ 8 min read · 🇰🇷 Seoul, Korea · Updated 2026

Seoul Street Food — Eat Everything

Seoul's street food scene is one of the great pleasures of visiting Korea. It's affordable, delicious, and eaten standing up at pojangmacha tents and street stalls at any hour of the day or night. The culture of eating on the street is deeply Korean — no pretension, maximum flavor, completely democratic. A ₩3,000 tteokbokki from a street cart is as satisfying as anything in a sit-down restaurant.

🍢 The Essential Seoul Street Foods

Tteokbokki (떡볶이) — The King

Chewy cylindrical rice cakes in a glossy, sweet-spicy gochujang sauce with fish cakes and boiled eggs. This is Korea's most beloved comfort food — served at school gates, market stalls, and dedicated restaurants. The sauce is a precise balance of sweet, spicy, and savory. Don't leave Seoul without eating it at least three times.

Price: ₩3,000–₩5,000 | Best spots: Myeongdong, Gwangjang Market, anywhere

Hotteok (호떡) — Sweet Pancake

Fried dough filled with brown sugar, cinnamon, and crushed nuts. Crispy outside, molten sweet inside. A winter Seoul street food staple, though available year-round. Order one and eat it immediately — the sugar filling is best when it's dangerously hot.

Price: ₩1,000–₩2,000 | Best spots: Insadong, Namdaemun Market

Twigim (튀김) — Korean Tempura

Deep-fried vegetables, squid, shrimp, and sweet potato in a light batter. Usually sold alongside tteokbokki — dip it in the spicy sauce for the full experience. Cheap, filling, satisfying.

Price: ₩500–₩1,000 per piece

Gimbap (김밥) — Korean Rice Roll

Rice and fillings wrapped in seaweed — similar to Japanese maki but distinctly Korean. Tuna, kimchi, bulgogi, or vegetable fillings. Eaten on the go. The triangle kimbap from convenience stores (GS25, 7-Eleven) is a staple Korean snack — ₩1,200 and genuinely good.

Price: ₩2,000–₩4,000 for a roll

Tornado Potato (회오리 감자)

A whole potato spiral-cut and fried on a skewer. Dusted with cheese, spicy, or original flavors. Completely mesmerizing to watch being made. Popular in tourist areas especially Myeongdong.

Price: ₩3,000–₩4,000

Egg Bread (계란빵)

A small sweet bread with a whole egg baked inside. Soft, slightly sweet, savory from the egg. Perfect cold-weather snack. Common near subway exits and markets.

Price: ₩1,000–₩2,000

💡 Street food tip: Most street food vendors don't have menus in English. Point at what other people are eating, hold up fingers for quantity, and have small bills ready. Smiling goes a long way. Most vendors have seen thousands of tourists and are patient.

📍 Best Street Food Areas

Myeongdong — Tourist Street Food Central

The main Myeongdong street fills with food stalls every evening from around 5pm. This is tourist-friendly street food — vendors often speak basic English, items are labeled, and everything is reasonably priced. Not the most authentic but extremely convenient and reliable.

Best items here: Tornado potato, lobster skewers, Korean fried chicken, dalgona coffee

Gwangjang Market (광장시장) — The Authentic One

Korea's oldest market and a genuine cultural institution. Go straight to the covered food hall in the center. Grandmothers who have been cooking the same dishes for decades serve bindaetteok (mung bean pancakes), mayak gimbap (addictive mini seaweed rolls with sesame sauce), yukhoe (raw beef), and more. This is Seoul street food at its most real.

Hours: 9am–11pm daily (food stalls busiest at lunch and early evening)

Namdaemun Market

Seoul's largest traditional market. The food section has incredible hotteok, pajeon (green onion pancake), and gimbap at very local prices. Less tourist-polished than Myeongdong — more authentic, slightly harder to navigate.

Pojangmacha Tents — Everywhere After Dark

Orange-tented street food stalls that appear at night throughout the city. Order tteokbokki, odeng (fish cake skewers in hot broth), and makgeolli (rice wine). The experience of standing at a pojangmacha in winter, warming your hands on a bowl of odeng broth, is quintessentially Korean.

💡 Market tip: At Gwangjang Market, the mayak gimbap stalls are legendary — look for the ajumma (older women) making them by hand. They're called mayak (narcotic) gimbap because they're addictively delicious. Order a plate (₩3,000) and you'll understand immediately.

🍺 Street Food & Drinks

  • Makgeolli (막걸리): Milky fermented rice wine. Slightly sweet, slightly sour, low alcohol. Buy in convenience stores for ₩1,500 or order at pojangmacha.
  • Soju: Korea's ubiquitous spirit. ₩1,500 at convenience stores. Mix with beer for somaek (the Korean boilermaker).
  • Sikhye (식혜): Sweet rice punch, non-alcoholic. Traditional and refreshing. Canned versions at convenience stores.
  • Street Coffee: Convenience store fresh-ground coffee machines — ₩1,000–₩1,500. Surprisingly good.

💰 Street Food Budget

  • Single street food item: ₩1,000–₩3,000
  • Full street food meal (3–4 items): ₩8,000–₩15,000
  • Gwangjang Market lunch: ₩10,000–₩20,000
  • Convenience store meal: ₩3,000–₩6,000
